title: De motu vibratorio laminarum elasticarum, ubi plures novae vibrationum species hactenus non pertractatae evolvuntur

deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler is deriving the equation of small transverse vibrations of an elastic lamina (a cantilever) that is clamped at A (x = a) and free at F (x = 0). On the previous page he balanced moments about a point Y. The inertial 'forces' acting on the segment FY, with load per unit length p = (K/2bk)·y_tt, produce a moment about Y equal to ∫_0^x (x−X) p(X) dX = ∫dx∫p dx. Both of these integrals vanish at x = 0 because no force acts beyond the free end.

This page:
(1) He equates that moment to the elastic restoring moment Kcc·y_xx, where Kcc is the bending stiffness (modern EI).
(2) He fixes the sign by a physical argument. With his conventions the inertial loads would straighten the lamina rather than sustain its curvature. Also, a lamina moving away from its natural straight state must be decelerated, not accelerated. Hence y_tt must enter with a minus sign: −(K/2bk)∫dx∫dx y_tt = Kcc y_xx, i.e. −∫dx∫dx y_tt = 2bkcc y_xx.
(3) He notes the coefficient is necessarily positive and sets 2bkcc = b^4.
(4) He differentiates twice in x, treating t as constant. The double integral is anchored at x = 0, so no constants are lost. This gives −∫dx y_tt = b^4 y_xxx and then −y_tt = b^4 y_xxxx. This is the Euler–Bernoulli dynamic beam equation y_tt + b^4 y_xxxx = 0, with b^4 = EI/(ρA) in modern terms.
(5) In §X he poses the task of finding y(x,t) satisfying this fourth-order PDE. He announces that he will first list the four boundary conditions. The next page gives them: y'' = y''' = 0 at the free end, y = y' = 0 at the clamped end.
errors: No mathematical error. The sign is fixed by a heuristic physical argument ('motion is retarded when leaving the natural state') rather than by a consistent sign convention for moments and curvature, but the resulting sign is correct. The double differentiation is legitimate because the integrals are taken from x = 0, which also yields the free-end conditions y'' = y''' = 0 used on the next page.

ideas.what: Dynamic equation of transverse vibration of an elastic beam derived from moment balance of inertial loads against bending moment Kcc·y''
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler and Daniel Bernoulli (1735–1744 static/modal forms). The PDE form is commonly credited to Euler in this memoir, E443.
ideas.where_published: E443 (Novi Comment. Petrop. 17, 1773). Modal (ordinary-differential) forms appear earlier in the Additamentum I of the Methodus inveniendi (E65, 1744). Discussed by Truesdell in Opera omnia II.11/2.

ideas.what: Converting an integral (moment) relation into a differential one by repeated differentiation, using lower limit x = 0 to encode the free-end conditions
ideas.modern_name: Equivalence of integral (shear/moment) and differential forms of beam equilibrium; natural boundary conditions at a free end
ideas.where_published: E443, continued on the next page

ideas.what: Abbreviation 2bkcc = b^4 so that the stiffness-to-mass ratio appears as a fourth power

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-known derivation of the Euler–Bernoulli beam PDE in E443, already analyzed by Truesdell. Nothing on this page is unrecorded.
transcription_corrections: The transcription matches the image. 'nanciſcimur' is printed slightly garbled ('nanciſcimur' with a damaged first letter). The last word of the page is the catchword 'tionis', continued on the next page.
